Mechanical properties of Fe–Al–M–C (M<sup>Z</sup>Ti, V, Nb, Ta)
alloys with strengthening carbides and Laves phase
L. Falat, A. Schneider*, G. Sauthoff, G. Frommeyer
Max-Planck-Institut fu¨r Eisenforschung GmbH, Max-Planck-Str. 1, Du¨sseldorf D-40237, Germany
Received 29 March 2004; received in revised form 15 May 2004; accepted 24 May 2004
Available online 26 April 2005
Abstract
The mechanical properties of Fe–15Al (in at.%) and Fe–26Al based alloys with alloying additions are investigated. The alloys contain
1 at.% C and 2 or 4 at.% Ti, V, Nb or Ta. Preliminary information on the mechanical properties of the investigated alloys is provided by
means of hardness tests. The mechanical testing of alloys is carried out in compression as well as in tension. Compression tests are carried out
at room temperature and at elevated temperatures including the temperature range of the yield stress anomaly. The tensile tests are performed
in order to determine the room temperature ductility and high temperature tensile strength at temperatures of possible industrial applications.
The investigation of the fracture surfaces of ruptured tensile specimens is performed by means of scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

1. Introduction
Iron–aluminium alloys are attractive for development of
structural materials for use in conventional power plants and
in the petrochemical industry, where materials with limited
density, reasonable strength and good corrosion resistance
are required [1–9]. Low materials costs are an additional
advantage for production of Fe–Al alloys. However, there is
a need to improve the room temperature ductility and high
temperature strength for application of these alloys.
The presence of carbides in Fe–Al alloys was rec-
ommended in several studies for a number of reasons.
Besides the precipitation strengthening effects, an improve-
ment of the room temperature ductility was observed
[10,11]. The studies [12,13] revealed a beneficial effect of
carbides on the machinability of iron aluminides. The hard
carbide particles in the Fe–Al matrix are also responsible for
an improvement of tribological (friction) properties such as
wear and erosion resistance [14]. The presence of Laves
phase in Fe–Al alloys is recommended due to its very
efficient strengthening effect [15–17]. On the other hand, the
intermetallic Laves phase precipitates are known to be very
brittle [18–20].
The present study concentrates on Fe(Al)-base and
Fe<sub>3</sub>Al-base alloys with strengthening precipitates, in
particular, on the mechanical behaviour of quaternary
Fe–15Al–2M–1C and Fe–26Al–(2 or 4)M–1C (M<sup>Z</sup>Ti, V,
Nb, Ta) alloys. The binary reference alloys (Fe–15Al and

Al have an A2 bcc disordered matrix up to the melting

order–disorder structural transitions, namely D0<sub>3</sub>/B2

2. Experimental procedure
The alloys were processed by vacuum induction melting.
The melts were cast into cylindrical copper moulds (32 mm
in diameter by 186 mm in length). For further details the
reader is referred to [21].
Brinell hardness was used with a load of 62.5 g and an
indentation ball with 2.5 mm diameter. For static mechanica
testing in uniaxial compression or tension, the samples were
cut from cast ingots by spark erosion. The dimensions of
compression samples were
( 6 \times 6 \times 1 0 ) ~ \mathrm { { m m } } ^ { 3 } .
For tensile
tests, flat samples of
( 3 . 5 \times 5 ) \ : \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }
cross-section with 15 mm
gauge length were used. All samples were cut in the direction
of the longitudinal axis of the ingot (casting direction). The
surfaces of the specimen were ground. All mechanical tests
were carried out at a deformation rate of
using a
ZWICK 1474 universal testing machine. The mechanical
tests at elevated temperatures were carried out in protective
argon atmosphere within a radiation furnace. In order to
stabilize the heat fluxes and the temperature field, the
samples for mechanical tests were held 30 min at the testing
temperature before loading. The testing temperature was
continuously checked by a NiCr–Ni thermocouple directly
on the surface of the test specimen. The fracture surfaces of
the tensile samples were investigated by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM-Hitachi S-530 with 20 kV, working
distance 15 mm) with secondary electrons (SE).

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Mechanical properties at room temperature
Fig. 1 shows the matrix Brinell hardness and the alloy
yield stress in compression of the investigated alloys.
According to the hardness measurements and compression
tests, all Fe–15Al–2M–1C alloys exhibit strengthening of
the Fe–Al matrix in comparison to the binary Fe–15Al alloy
(Fig. 1a). On the other hand, for Fe–26Al–(2 or 4)M–1C
alloys, hardening and also softening effects in comparison to
the binary Fe–26Al alloy were revealed by the hardness
tests (Fig. 1b). The alloys with V, Nb or Ta show higher
hardness than the binary Fe–26Al alloy, whereas the alloys
containing Ti are softened. The softening effects of Ti in a
single phase
\mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { A l }
based alloys were also reported in
another study [22].

There is a good correlation between hardness and yield
stress in compression for Fe–15Al based alloys with Ti and
V (Fig. 1a). On the other hand, the alloy Fe–15Al–2Nb–1C
has higher hardness, but lower yield stress than the alloy
Fe–15Al–2Ta–1C.
The matrix hardness values of most Fe–26Al based
alloys do not correlate with values of yield stress in
compression (Fig. 1b). Except alloy Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C, all
other Fe–26Al based alloys exhibit lower yield stress in
compression than the binary Fe–26Al alloy.
Fig. 2 shows the engineering stress–strain curves for the
investigated alloys at room temperature in compression. The
plastic deformation of Fe–15Al–2M–1C alloys shows
parabolic work hardening behaviour (Fig. 2a), which is

typical for most disordered polycrystalline metallic
materials. The alloys containing Nb or Ta show the highest
strengthening effects. The hardening of binary Fe–15Al
alloy is low and almost linear.
The deformation behaviour of Fe–26Al–(2 or 4)M–1C
alloys (Fig. 2b) exhibits very high strengthening with almost
constant hardening rates, until a final stage of parabolic
work hardening is reached. The stress–strain curve of the
binary Fe–26Al alloy consist of a linear elastic part,
followed by a parabolic hardening stage. Despite lower
yield stresses of most Fe–26Al based alloys in comparison
to the binary alloy, all these alloys exhibit much stronger
hardening effects during plastic deformation.
Fig. 3 represents the engineering stress–strain curves of
the investigated alloys at room temperature in tension. The
ductility of most Fe–Al–M–C alloys is very poor. Some
alloys crack even during elastic deformation. Apart from the
binary Fe–15Al alloy, the highest values of total elongation
were obtained for the alloys Fe–15Al–2Ti–1C and
Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C, respectively.

Fig. 3 represents the engineering stress–strain curves of

The mechanical properties of investigated alloys tested at
room temperature are summarised in Table 2. The tensile
tests of both Fe–15Al-based and Fe–26Al-based alloys
revealed an earlier onset of plastic deformation than during
compression tests, i.e. the values of yield stresses in
compression are higher than those in tension. This
phenomenon—the so-called tension–compression asymme-
try is known in metals with bcc crystal structure [23–26].
The tension–compression asymmetry has primarily been
related to the glide of the screw dislocations with nonplanar
(delocalised) core structure [27,28]. Another factor con-
tributing to the tension–compression asymmetry could be
the Bauschinger effect, which originates from the different
elastic properties of matrix and secondary phases resulting
in internal tensions during solidification of alloys. Another
significant contribution to the asymmetric tension–com-
pression behaviour is related to the notch sensitivity of the
matrix due to the presence of precipitates. In such a case the
morphology of the precipitate is the controlling factor for
the notching effect in the matrix. Indeed, the alloy Fe–26Al–
2V–1C with relatively thin (about 0.5 mm in thickness) and
sharp plate-like vanadium carbide precipitates shows a
pronounced tension–compression asymmetry (<sup>z</sup>36%).

In Fig. 4, SEM-fractographs of investigated alloys are
shown. The binary Fe–15Al alloy with ductility of 16%, was
fractured with transgranular fracture with very fine cleavage
facets (Fig. 4a). All Fe–15Al–2M–1C alloys were fractured
with coarse transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4b–e), which
corresponds to their brittle behaviour. The alloy Fe–15Al–
2Ti–1C exhibits the highest room-temperature ductility
(<sup>z</sup>3.3%) of all Fe–15Al-based alloys. The binary Fe–26Al
alloy exhibits a very coarse transgranular fracture (Fig. 4f).
The alloy Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C which has the highest ductility
(<sup>z</sup>1.4%) of all Fe–26Al based alloys, exhibits a very fine
facetted transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4j). The fracture
surface of the alloy Fe–26Al–2V–1C with uniform steps
indicates transgranular fracture (Fig. 4i), with the influence
of the crystallographic orientation of plate-like vanadium
carbide precipitates. The orientation relationship of these
vanadium carbide precipitates with the matrix was deter-
mined in a previous study [21]. According to this result, it
can be stated that the fracture facets are formed on the (001)
planes of the matrix which are parallel to the (001) planes of
the precipitates. For the other Fe–26Al-based alloys a more
complex fracture was observed. The fracture surfaces of the
alloys with Ti or Ta are partially intergranular and
transgranular (Fig. 4g–l). The smooth fracture areas
correspond to the decohesion and the facetted areas to the
cleavage. On the intergranular fracture areas of the alloys
Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C and Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C the cube-like TiC
precipitates can be clearly distinguished. The alloy Fe–26Al–
4Ti–1C was fractured almost completely with intergranular
decohesion. The alloy Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C showed intergra-
nular decohesion besides transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4k).
On the intergranular fracture areas many densely distributed
precipitates are observed. These precipitates disturbed
the intergranular fracture surface so significantly that the
decohesion areas are not smooth as usually but rough. The
alloys Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C and Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C show totally
brittle behaviour at room temperature.

2Ti–1C exhibits the highest room-temperature ductility
(<sup>z</sup>3.3%) of all Fe–15Al-based alloys. The binary Fe–26Al
alloy exhibits a very coarse transgranular fracture (Fig. 4f).
The alloy Fe–26Al–2Nb–1C which has the highest ductility
(<sup>z</sup>1.4%) of all Fe–26Al based alloys, exhibits a very fine
facetted transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4j). The fracture
surface of the alloy Fe–26Al–2V–1C with uniform steps
indicates transgranular fracture (Fig. 4i), with the influence
of the crystallographic orientation of plate-like vanadium
carbide precipitates. The orientation relationship of these
vanadium carbide precipitates with the matrix was deter-
mined in a previous study [21]. According to this result, it
can be stated that the fracture facets are formed on the (001)
planes of the matrix which are parallel to the (001) planes of
the precipitates. For the other Fe–26Al-based alloys a more
complex fracture was observed. The fracture surfaces of the
alloys with Ti or Ta are partially intergranular and
transgranular (Fig. 4g–l). The smooth fracture areas
correspond to the decohesion and the facetted areas to the
cleavage. On the intergranular fracture areas of the alloys
Fe–26Al–2Ti–1C and Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C the cube-like TiC
precipitates can be clearly distinguished. The alloy Fe–26Al–
4Ti–1C was fractured almost completely with intergranular
decohesion. The alloy Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C showed intergra-
nular decohesion besides transgranular cleavage (Fig. 4k).
On the intergranular fracture areas many densely distributed
precipitates are observed. These precipitates disturbed
the intergranular fracture surface so significantly that the
decohesion areas are not smooth as usually but rough. The
alloys Fe–26Al–4Ti–1C and Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C show totally
brittle behaviour at room temperature.

4. Summary and conclusions
Addition of alloying elements such as carbon and
transition metals to Fe–Al alloys leads to strengthening or
softening effects on hardness and yield stress of the
investigated Fe–Al–M–C (M<sup>Z</sup>Ti, V, Nb, Ta) alloys at
room temperature. All Fe–15Al-based and Fe–26Al-based
alloys exhibit higher hardening rates during plastic defor-
mation than corresponding binary Fe–Al alloys. The alloys
with Nb or Ta show the highest strengthening effects. Most
investigated Fe–Al–M–C alloys have been found to be rather
brittle at room temperature. The fracture surface observations
revealed two different fracture modes, namely: transgranular
cleavage (TGC) and intergranular decohesion (IGD). Apart
from the binary Fe–15Al alloy, the highest values of room
temperature ductility were obtained for the alloys Fe–15Al–
2Ti–1C (<sup>z</sup>3.3%) and Fe–26Al–2Nb–

4. Summary and conclusions
Addition of alloying elements such as carbon and
transition metals to Fe–Al alloys leads to strengthening or
softening effects on hardness and yield stress of the
investigated Fe–Al–M–C (M<sup>Z</sup>Ti, V, Nb, Ta) alloys at
room temperature. All Fe–15Al-based and Fe–26Al-based
alloys exhibit higher hardening rates during plastic defor-
mation than corresponding binary Fe–Al alloys. The alloys
with Nb or Ta show the highest strengthening effects. Most
investigated Fe–Al–M–C alloys have been found to be rather
brittle at room temperature. The fracture surface observations
revealed two different fracture modes, namely: transgranular
cleavage (TGC) and intergranular decohesion (IGD). Apart
from the binary Fe–15Al alloy, the highest values of room
temperature ductility were obtained for the alloys Fe–15Al–
2Ti–1C (<sup>z</sup>3.3%) and Fe–26Al–2Nb–
C \left( \approx 1 . 4 \% \right)
At elevated temperatures all investigated Fe–Al–M–C
alloys exhibit strengthening effects in comparison to the
corresponding binary reference alloys. Mechanical testing
in compression at various temperatures revealed the usual
decrease of the yield stresses with increasing temperature
for the Fe–15Al-based alloys. The alloys containing Nb or
Ta show the highest strength at all tested temperatures. All
Fe–26Al-based alloys exhibit an anomalous increase in
strength within a certain range of intermediate
temperatures—the yield stress anomaly. It was found that
the alloying elements Ti or V have no significant influence
on the position of the yield stress anomaly peak, whereas for
the alloys with Nb or Ta the peak is shifted towards lower
temperatures. Only the alloy Fe–26Al–4Nb–1C was found
to show a substantial strengthening effect on the yield stress
at the peak maximum (619 MPa compared to other alloys—
ca. 400 MPa). This result demonstrates the strengthening
efficiency of Laves phase. All investigated alloys exhibit
a tension–compression asymmetry at room temperature as
well as at elevated temperatures. The tension–compression
asymmetry of Fe–26Al-based alloys is higher than that of
Fe–15Al-based alloys. The obtained results show promising
properties of the Fe–Al alloys containing Nb or Ta and C for
high temperature application.
